name: Nikhil Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's about three days of lectures, one long lab on Thursday, and then whatever I can fit around ten hours a week on the desk at the campus library. I share a flat on Dunmore Road with three guys, and we take turns cooking, badly. I'm doing computer science. Week five, and I'm finally at the point where the maths lectures make sense.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you finding the programming side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than I expected. I did a bit of coding at school, so the first assignments were fine, but the group project is humbling. Four of us, one repository, and everybody's code looks different. I've started to use an AI tool now and then, mostly to explain error messages I don't understand. I don't paste its answers in, I just read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that matches what I've seen. It's useful for explaining an error or tidying a paragraph, and that's about it. I'd probably get a few jokes from friends who've bet their whole career on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be a bit relieved but not wildly. My degree stays worth roughly what it was, and the junior job market stays as tough as it already is. My parents are paying part of my rent, and I'd still want to repay them by getting a decent first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and keep the library job. I'd do one small project for my portfolio each term, like the timetable app I've started. And I'd carry on using the AI tool sparingly, since it saves a little time and I'm learning when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, really. There's the normal stress of exams and money, but nothing that feels out of my hands. It's the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using the AI tool sparingly. How do you decide when to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum runs a small physiotherapy clinic, and she's the one who'd benefit most from boring AI, like appointment reminders. She says her receptionist spends an hour a day on phone calls that software could do. In this world, I'd guess that's about where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your mum's clinic come into this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change my plans, but I would keep one eye on the junior jobs. Last year only about half of the second-years from my course got a placement, so I'm already worried about that, with or without AI. It's a competition regardless of how smart the tools are.

say: I'd say it **matches what I've seen**: useful for small jobs, not a revolution.
I'd joke with friends who bet their whole career on it.
think: My degree keeps **about the same value**, and the junior market stays tough.
I still want a decent **first job** to repay my parents.
do: Keep studying and the **library desk job**.
Build one **portfolio project** each term, starting with my timetable app.
Keep using the AI tool **sparingly** to learn when it's wrong.
feel: **Calm**, with the usual exam and money stress.
S0.quote: Last year only about half of the second-years from my course got a placement, so I'm already worried about that, with or without AI.
fieldNote: Nikhil is **calm** because the main worry, the placement market, exists with or without AI.
He is a measured, selective AI user who reads answers rather than pasting them.
His mum's clinic is a good small example of **boring AI** that saves an hour a day.

steps.text: Keep the ten-hour library desk job
Finish the timetable app as a portfolio project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this needs a plan. If AI starts doing the coding and checking in many jobs, then a computer science degree isn't automatically a ticket. I'd argue for retraining funds paid for by taxing the companies that profit, and I'd say that online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my course is right in the splash zone. Junior coders do the simple tasks, and those are exactly what the tools do well. I'd say there's maybe a one in three chance I end up unemployed for a spell after graduating, and that would hit me and my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in a bit more on the tools, because I'd rather be the person who can supervise the tools than the person they replace. I'd pick modules on databases and systems, which are harder to replace. And I'd apply for a placement early, in my second year, instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. I'm not in panic, since there's time and I can adjust. But it's like seeing the queue for the exit get longer while you're still deciding to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean in on the tools. What does that look like in a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first-year jobs are what worries me, because companies could just not replace the juniors who leave. Most people still have work in this picture, though, so I'm not predicting disaster. It's about being near the front of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Mira about choosing a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Mira is fifteen and thinking about doing computing too. I'd tell her to choose something she'd enjoy even if the job market changes, because that matters more than a label. I wouldn't tell her to avoid it.

say: I'd say a computer science degree is **not automatically a ticket** any more.
I'd argue for **retraining funds** paid by the companies that profit.
think: My course sits in the **splash zone**, because junior coding tasks are easy for tools.
I could face a **spell without work** after graduating, which also hits my parents.
do: Learn the AI tools better so I can **supervise** them.
Pick **database and systems modules**, which are harder to replace.
Apply for a **placement early**, in second year.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching the exit queue grow while deciding.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who can supervise the tools than the person they replace.
fieldNote: Nikhil's answer is **practical and numerical**, giving a rough one-in-three chance of a jobless spell.
He chooses to learn the tools instead of avoiding them, in line with his steady adaptability.
He cares about his sister's course choice and gives **balanced advice**.

steps.text: Spend one evening a week building projects with AI tools
Choose database and systems modules for second year
Back a campaign for company-funded retraining
Apply for a second-year placement by January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and the first thing to fix is who pays. If most thinking work goes to machines by 2028, we need some public income support fast. I'd say that on the student forums, and I'd vote for anyone who treats it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel my plans fall apart. I'd have been at university for one year, and the jobs I'm training for would be vanishing before I finish. I'd be anxious about my parents' money as well, because the clinic's earnings depend on people having jobs and insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the degree for now, because I'd have nowhere better to put the time. But I'd stop planning around a tech job and ask my mum what a hands-on career like physiotherapy would really involve. I'd also look at electrical work. I'd talk to her about that this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's less a feeling of disaster and more of the ground tilting. I can still make choices, but each choice feels like a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop planning around a tech job. What would you plan around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also stop spending on small things, like the weekend train home. The library job becomes more important, so I'd ask for extra hours. If my parents lose clients, they might stop helping with rent, and I'd need to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardest conversation would be with my dad, who's a surveyor and has always said the degree is the safe route. I'd tell him straight that I don't think that's true now, and ask what he'd do in my place. He'd probably be quiet for a while.

say: I'd say we're **not ready**, and the first question is who pays.
I'd call for **public income support** and back anyone serious about it.
think: My plans would **fall apart**, because the jobs I'm training for may vanish.
My parents' **money** depends on clients having jobs, so their help could stop.
do: Stay on the degree but stop planning around a **tech job**.
Ask the library for **extra hours** and cut small spending.
Talk to Mum about **hands-on careers** like physiotherapy.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground is tilting and each choice is a guess.
S2.quote: I'd stop planning around a tech job and ask my mum what a hands-on career like physiotherapy would really involve.
fieldNote: Nikhil reacts by **re-planning**, not freezing, and quickly shifts towards hands-on fields.
His worry reaches his parents' money because the clinic depends on **other people's jobs**.
The conversation with his surveyor dad shows a family belief in degrees being safe.

steps.text: Ask Mum to let me shadow a day at the clinic
Skip the monthly train home and cook more
Ask the library manager for ten more hours
Sign up to the student campaign for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us a real chance to build safety nets, but only if politicians start now. Five years is about one election and a half. I'd say that to friends and probably post about it, which sounds smug, but I'd do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have around two years of work before it bites. I'd graduate in 2029, and AGI is 2031. That's enough to repay something and get experience, but not enough to feel settled. I'd treat the first job as a bridge, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take the best placement I can. I'd save as much as I can in those two working years, and I'd keep options open, maybe a part-time course in something hands-on like electrical installation. And I'd stop assuming my parents will keep helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think, and a bit restless. It's not the cold fear of the two-year one. It's the sense of having a short window, and I want to use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called the first job a bridge. What would make a good bridge job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bridge idea is important. If I know I'll be in a job for two years, I won't worry about the title or the ladder. I'd choose the place where I learn the most and earn the most, even if it's a boring company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mum and dad might give different advice. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say to follow my curiosity, and my dad would say to take the safe job. I'd probably split the difference: take the safe job, and spend my evenings on the curious stuff. It's what I do now with the library and the timetable app.

say: I'd say it's a **real chance** to build safety nets, but only if politicians start now.
I'd post about it online, though I know that **sounds smug**.
think: I'd have about **two years of work** after graduating in 2029 before 2031.
I'd treat the first job as a **bridge**, not a career.
do: Finish the degree and take the **best placement** I can.
**Save** as much as possible during those two working years.
Start a part-time course in a **hands-on trade** like electrical installation.
feel: **Uneasy** and restless, with a short window to use well.
S3.quote: If I know I'll be in a job for two years, I won't worry about the title or the ladder.
fieldNote: Nikhil frames the first job as a **bridge**, a practical way to live with a known deadline.
He splits his parents' advice into a plan: a safe job plus evening curiosity.
His timeline is precise, with graduation in 2029 and AGI in 2031 shaping his choices.

steps.text: Save half of every first-job pay cheque
Pick the placement that pays most and teaches most
Start an evening electrical installation course after graduating
Tell Mum and Dad not to expect repayment help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a sensible country to adjust, and I'd use my vote for it. I'd also say my generation shouldn't be the only one expected to retrain. Older workers and companies have to move as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of people would drift and say 'it's fine' for eight years. Ten years makes it feel optional. I'd be in the middle of a career by then, around 28, with maybe a mortgage, which is exactly when a change would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, build up real experience, and keep a skill outside coding, probably something with people, like project management. I'd stay in a flat share longer to save more. And I'd try to learn how the tools work underneath, not only how to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine. The long timeline means I can plan, which suits me. I do better with a clear date and a to-do list than with sudden surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lot of people would drift. Would you be one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One thing I'd watch is my parents' retirement. In ten years they're near it, and if prices and pensions shift because of AGI, that matters more to me than my own job. I'd probably ask them about their savings in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would your parents' retirement matter more than your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell friends to relax, but I wouldn't tell them to panic either. I'd say plans are better than predictions, so build a bit of savings and a second skill, and watch what your employer does with the tools.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough to adjust**, and older workers and companies must move too.
I'd tell friends to build **savings** and a **second skill**.
think: Many people would **drift** for eight years, because ten years makes it feel optional.
A change at **28**, maybe with a mortgage, would hurt the most.
do: Build **real experience** and a second skill like project management.
Stay in a **flat share** longer to save more.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine; a clear timeline suits me.
S4.quote: Plans are better than predictions, so build a bit of savings and a second skill, and watch what your employer does with the tools.
fieldNote: Nikhil prefers **plans over predictions** and uses a long timeline as a to-do list.
He is honest that he might drift too, which is a small self-aware moment.
He links the long scenario to his parents' **retirement and savings**, a family stake.

steps.text: Stay in a flat share to save a deposit
Learn how language models work, not only how to use them
Take a project management certificate within five years
Ask Mum and Dad about their pension plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to prepare and my parents' money gets tangled up with mine. What would help is a clear public plan, like income support and funded retraining, announced before it's needed. Students would also need a say in how loans work if jobs disappear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that I'm not scared of the technology. I'm worried about whether the people running things will share what it produces, and I think that's a political choice, not a technical one.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the technology. I'm worried about whether the people running things will share what it produces
portrait: Nikhil is an **18-year-old** computer science student who shares a flat and works ten hours a week at the campus library.
His mum runs a physiotherapy clinic and his dad is a **surveyor**; they pay part of his costs.
He is progressive and a **steady** adapter who uses AI tools sparingly and checks what they say.
He plans with numbers and dates, treating a first job as a **bridge** in the faster scenarios.
He sees the problem as **political**, about who shares the gains, and says so.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, since there'd be no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** announced early: income support, funded retraining and fair rules on student loans.
